overview: Tuvaluan island communities maintain shared ceremonies, craft skills and food production alongside overseas connections. Island traditions and the modern independent state require distinct historical timelines.

items.text: Maneapa meeting halls host cultural ceremonies and gatherings through the year. They remain places where community traditions are performed.
Local makers produce fans, mats, baskets, necklaces, woodcarvings and fishhooks. The Women's Handicraft Centre and island sellers connect this work with contemporary exchange.
Rainwater stored in tanks supplies households in a landscape without rivers or lakes. Water storage is a practical adaptation to island conditions.
Fishing and cultivation provide daily food, alongside cash incomes and remittances from people working overseas. Marine resources and coconut products also enter exchange.
Samoan London Missionary Society teaching reached the islands in the 1860s. Christianity became influential while many earlier traditions continued.
Tuvalu became an independent constitutional monarchy on 1 October 1978. That state transition did not begin Tuvaluan community history.
